newsitem.title: USA: Dow Jones cuts top executives' bonuses.
newsitem.headline: Dow Jones cuts top executives' bonuses.

text.p: Bonuses for Dow Jones & Co.'s top executives were cut after the company's compensation committee determined its stock performance in the past year was not satisfactory.

According to the proxy statement filed by the publisher of the Wall Street Journal in advance of its April 16 annual meeting and made available Monday, Chairman and Chief Executive Peter Kann had his annual bonus cut to $380,000 for 1996 compared with $445,000 in the prior year.

The Independent Association of Publishers' Employees, which represents employees at Dow Jones, including the Wall Street Journal and Barron's, also has put forth a stockholder proposal to create an independent review of top management and their performance.
In the proxy statement, the compansation committee reported that it compared Dow Jones' performance in 1996 with companies in the S&P 500 as well as the S&P's publishing and newspapers index.

"Overall, the committee determined that performance for the 1993-1996 period was less than fully satisfactory, particularly as measured by three financial criteria given significant weight by the committee: stock price performance, total stockholder return and return on equity," it said.

Dow Jones President and Chief Operating Officer Kenneth Burenga's bonus was cut to $270,000 from $310,000; Senior Vice President Carl Valenti's was reduced to $155,000 from $220,000; and Senior Vice President Peter Skinner's dropped to $165,000 from $205,000.
Only Senior Vice President James Ottaway Jr's remained unchanged at $160,000.
The union-backed stockholder proposal was to be voted on at the annual meeting. The union holds 55 shares of Dow Jones' common stock and 10 shares of its Class B common stock.
Dow Jones has 73.9 million shares of common stock and 21.6 million shares of Class B common stock outstanding.
Separately, Standard & Poors lowered Dow Jones' corporate credit ratings and senior unsecured debt rating to AA-minus from AA, and said its outlook for Dow Jones is now negative.

Analysts said they were not surprised by the downgrading given the negative publicity that has poured out of Dow Jones in recent months as some family members who control the company have expressed dissatisfaction with its stock performance.
It also followed recent news from the company that it would spend about $650 million to revamp its Telerate financial information services unit, now renamed Dow Jones Markets.

"It does concern what we know: that they're going to have some earnings constraints," Smith Barney analyst John Reidy said of the downgrading. He added that the new rating level was still competitive with other media companies.

Union President Ron Chen, a copy editor at the Wall Street Journal, said "For some time, the union and the people who work here at Dow Jones have recognised there's something wrong with this company... We have been trying to somehow get the world to take a look at this company and find out what's going on".
The board of directors has opposed the union's proposal, saying it believed it was "unnecessary in light of the board's current policies and practices regarding executive compensation."
Dow Jones competes against Reuters Holdings Plc and Bloomberg LP in major financial markets.
Dow Jones stock closed 12.5 cents lower at $42.875 on the New York Stock Exchange. Its high for the last year is $46.125 vs. a low of $31.875.
